title: Linux User Management and File Permission Hardening
description: Students create users and groups, assign file permissions using octal and symbolic notation, discover SUID misconfigurations, and practice privilege escalation concepts on an Ubuntu VM — building the foundation for understanding Linux access control.
objective: Students will create a multi-user environment with appropriate file permissions, identify dangerous SUID binaries, demonstrate how permission misconfigurations lead to privilege escalation, and fix each misconfiguration they create.

steps.title: Create Users, Groups, and a Shared Directory
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on your Ubuntu VM. You will set up a realistic multi-user environment.

**Create two new users:**
```bash
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash alice
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash bob
sudo passwd alice    # set a memorable test password
sudo passwd bob
```

**Create a shared group and add both users:**
```bash
sudo groupadd webteam
sudo usermod -aG webteam alice
sudo usermod -aG webteam bob
# Verify membership:
groups alice
groups bob
```

**Create a shared project directory:**
```bash
sudo mkdir -p /var/project/shared
sudo chown alice:webteam /var/project/shared
sudo chmod 2770 /var/project/shared
# 2770 = setgid bit + rwxrws---
# The setgid bit makes all files created inside inherit the 'webteam' group
ls -la /var/project/
```

Take a screenshot of the `ls -la /var/project/` output. The shared directory should show `rwxrws---` and be owned by `alice:webteam`.

steps.title: Test Permission Boundaries
steps.instructions:
Switch between user accounts to verify that permissions work as intended.

**Switch to alice and create a file in the shared directory:**
```bash
su - alice
cd /var/project/shared
echo 'Alice wrote this' > alice-file.txt
ls -la
```
Note: the file's group should automatically be `webteam` (because of setgid).

**Switch to bob and test access:**
```bash
su - bob
cat /var/project/shared/alice-file.txt   # Should succeed (group read)
echo 'Bob edited this' >> /var/project/shared/alice-file.txt   # Should succeed (group write)
ls -la /var/project/shared/
```

**Test that an outside user cannot access the directory:**
```bash
su - $(whoami)    # Go back to your admin user (exit from bob)
# Create a user NOT in webteam:
sudo useradd -m outsider
su - outsider
ls /var/project/shared/    # Should show 'Permission denied'
cat /var/project/shared/alice-file.txt   # Should also fail
exit
```

Document each access attempt and whether it succeeded or failed. Explain why each result is correct based on the permissions set.

steps.title: Create and Investigate Dangerous Permissions
steps.instructions:
Intentionally create security misconfigurations so you can see their impact.

**Misconfiguration 1 — World-writable sensitive file:**
```bash
sudo mkdir -p /opt/appdata
echo 'DB_PASSWORD=SuperSecret123' | sudo tee /opt/appdata/config.env
sudo chmod 777 /opt/appdata/config.env
ls -la /opt/appdata/
```
Switch to `outsider` and read the file:
```bash
su - outsider
cat /opt/appdata/config.env   # Succeeds — everyone can read!
exit
```

**Misconfiguration 2 — SUID on a custom script:**
```bash
sudo bash -c 'echo "#!/bin/bash" > /tmp/whoami-test.sh && echo "id && whoami" >> /tmp/whoami-test.sh'
sudo chmod 4755 /tmp/whoami-test.sh   # SUID set, owned by root
/tmp/whoami-test.sh   # Should run as root even when called by normal user
```

**Find all SUID files on the system:**
```bash
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | sort
```
Capture this output. Identify any SUID files in unusual locations (not /bin, /usr/bin, /usr/sbin, /usr/lib).

steps.title: Fix the Misconfigurations
steps.instructions:
Apply the principle of least privilege to correct each issue.

**Fix 1 — Correct the config file permissions:**
```bash
sudo chmod 640 /opt/appdata/config.env
sudo chown root:webteam /opt/appdata/config.env
ls -la /opt/appdata/config.env
# Now: -rw-r----- root webteam
```
Verify outsider can no longer read it:
```bash
su - outsider
cat /opt/appdata/config.env   # Should now fail with 'Permission denied'
exit
```

**Fix 2 — Remove the dangerous SUID bit:**
```bash
sudo chmod 755 /tmp/whoami-test.sh   # Remove SUID (4 prefix)
ls -la /tmp/whoami-test.sh
# Should now show -rwxr-xr-x (no 's')
```

**Best practice — Audit and document:**
Create a simple security checklist. Run these audit commands and document the output:
```bash
# World-writable files outside /tmp (potential security issues)
find / -xdev -perm -002 -not -path '/tmp/*' -not -path '/var/tmp/*' 2>/dev/null

# Files with no owner (potential orphaned malware)
find / -xdev -nouser 2>/dev/null

# Recently modified system files (forensic indicator)
find /etc /bin /usr/bin -newer /etc/passwd -type f 2>/dev/null
```

steps.title: Document Findings in a Security Report
steps.instructions:
Compile your findings into a brief security audit report.

Your report should include the following sections (can be in your PDF submission):

**Section 1 — Environment Setup**
- List the users created and their group memberships
- Show the shared directory permissions and explain the setgid bit

**Section 2 — Permission Boundary Tests**
- Table showing each user, which file/directory they attempted to access, and the result

**Section 3 — Vulnerability Discovery**
- Screenshot of the world-writable config file being read by outsider
- Screenshot of SUID script running with elevated privileges
- List of all SUID binaries found on the system

**Section 4 — Remediation**
- Before and after `ls -la` for each fix applied
- One paragraph explaining the principle of least privilege in your own words

**Final reflection question:** If an attacker gained code execution as the `www-data` user (a common web server compromise), which of the SUID binaries on your system would be most dangerous, and why? Reference GTFOBins (https://gtfobins.github.io/) if you need help identifying risky binaries.

expected_output: Students submit: (1) A PDF report with all 4 sections completed. (2) Screenshots of: shared directory permissions, permission boundary tests (success and failure), world-writable vulnerability exploitation, SUID script execution, and all fixes applied. (3) A table of discovered SUID binaries with any risky ones identified. (4) Written answers to the reflection question.
